utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before we begin, there's a matter I want to deal with in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me remind everybody, with this microphone there need to be pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is associated with this witness who will be known throughout as B-1120 or 1120, I suppose, for convenience, a -- an exhibit of seven tabs -- six tabs, beg your pardon, and the last tab has at the top of it the name of the witness. If that can simply be shown to him. It's obviously an exhibit that must remain under seal Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just, please, Witness B-1120, confirm that that name at the top of the list is yours by saying yes if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the exhibit be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P492.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness's evidence is for the most part admitted under the provisions of 92 bis by way of testimony on the former occasion. I summarise the effect of his evidence which relates, as the Chamber knows, to Foca. I shall read only some of the paragraphs in the summary provided or read from only some of the paragraphs in the summary provided to the Chamber. Paragraph 2. SDS leaders such as Karadzic, Plavsic and others made statements at the material time to the effect that Serbs and Muslims could no longer live together and spread messages of hate and false propaganda over the radio, examples being how at a rally in 1990, Vojislav Maksimovic stated that Muslim blood would flow again down the Drina and Cehotina rivers as it had done down the Drina in the Second World War. In April 1992, another example. Miro Stanic said that it was time to clear up once and for all relations with Muslims it being impossible to live with them. Radovan Karadzic saying at a parliamentary session shortly before the war that there is a threat that Muslims in Bosnia could disappear from the country. The war, as far as Foca is concerned started, started on 7th of April of 1992 when the JNA assisted by Territorial Defence forces and paramilitaries took over the municipality occupying it, setting fire to Muslim houses and destroying 30 or so mosques. The witness was arrested, taken first to a military or former military warehouse and then transferred to the local KP Dom or prison where a couple of days after his arrival a soldier from Serbia wrote names, surnames, and professions of detainees, the witness staying at that location until July of 1993. In April or May of 1992, some 25 to 30 Muslims tried to escape from the village of Jelec to avoid being arrested, sought protection from the JNA at the Kalinovik barracks and instead of being protected were taken by the JNA from there to be detained at the KP Dom. Paragraph 13 is new evidence that I will just deal with very briefly if I may through the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1120, did you from information provided to you by a man called Celik, learn of Muslims having escaped and fled to Montenegro, being followed there by members of the SDS leadership including Vojislav Maksimovic and Miro Stanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Celik inform you that the SDS leadership demanded their return, criticising Momir Bulatovic for sheltering them and they were eventually returned or at least 21 of them were returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. The rest were returned in cars, and this was a larger group consisting of 21 men that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I return to the summary. Paragraph 15 or 14 and 15. The witness was interrogated but not particularly mistreated. Others were. Go on to paragraph 18. Nutrition at the KP Dom was very poor. Serb prisoners were better treated than was this witness and others like him. Detainees suffered various things including lice as a result of not being able to have any form of hygiene really and he lost a very considerable amount of weight, 20 kilogrammes as paragraph 24 reveals, having to go through the cold of the winter where there was snow on the ground in large quantities without anyway of keeping warm. Paragraph 21. Several prisoners died of the conditions actually in the course of their detention. Others died after their release. Paragraph 25. There was a systematic ill-treatment of non-Serbs at the KP Dom. The witness himself was taken to isolation cells on two occasions for arbitrary reasons and then beaten by a Serb guard. Paragraph 2, some 35 detainees were taken between the 13th and the 30th of June from the place where they were kept at the KP Dom. They didn't return. The witness and others heard sounds at the relevant times of beatings and of shootings and indeed of people or things being thrown into the river nearby. Other prisoners were taken out for sessions of interrogations and beatings. Some of them simply never returning. The beatings, of course, paragraph 31, created an atmosphere of terrible fear. In May 1992, the doctor in charge at the KP Dom made an observation about the danger of being there by reference to the fact that for every Serb killed, three to five Muslims would disappear. The witness's evidence is to the effect that of the 600 or so detainees that passed through KP Dom, about 400 disappeared, about 240 survived or are known to have survived. In September 1992, a large number of prisoners were taken out under the pretext that they were going to pick plums in Ustikolina. They were never seen again, the 45 of them. Paragraph 36 is new.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1120, were you aware of a mass grave that was uncovered as late as the end of the trial at which you earlier gave evidence? Just yes or no to that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will do. Did you notice the heads of the bodies that were found in the mass grave had typical marks indicating how they had died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. In the same places on the heads or skulls, there were openings of roughly the same size, which was indicative of the method of execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Namely gunshot. And did you also observe ropes present suggestive of or showing that detainees had been tied up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, there were ropes. A special kind of rope used for parachutes, quite a strong one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move on with the summary, paragraph 37. The warden of KP Dom, Krnojelac, indicated that they were given orders by higher command, he saying that nothing could be done. And paragraph 39 speaking of a meeting in Bijeljina with all other commanders of detention camps similar to the KP Dom where again discussion was held about the fact that decisions were made at a level, so he asserted, higher than his. We now come to paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1120 -- I think the summary may be wrong as to the dates here; I'll ask the witness. In an early part of 1993, were there three Cengic cousins, Nezir, Hilmo, and Fehim, elderly men who were detained at the KP Dom and you discovered or learnt that they were called to the warden's office? If so, what month or months of 1993 do you understand this to have happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. This was January or February 1993. Closer to January than February. Around 16th of January, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard about this. Well, we'll discover where you heard about this in a moment, but as a result of going to the warden's office, did they discover that - just yes or no to this - intervention had occurred and that they were due to be released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not withstanding the fact that they were to be released by way it may be of exchange, paragraph 41, did they have fear as a result of what they'd been told Muslims generally in detention could expect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. They returned after a lengthy conversation. Prior to leaving for Belgrade, they came back full of fear. They were shaking all over as if they were suffering from Parkinson's disease. They said that next to Krnojelac was Commander Marko Kovac who said that this was a chance for the Serbs. We must settle accounts with the Muslims for good, though he regretted that he was under the pressure of a powerful figure so he had to do this. I'm referring to the exchange of these three men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to that powerful figure in a minute, but just to complete the story, paragraph 42. Were those three cousins, as you understood it, picked up by a guard the following day, taken to Belgrade for an exchange, and did you get confirmation of this story after the event because you met the Cengic cousins, or at least one of them, subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. After I was exchanged and when I reached Sarajevo, this was confirmed by a brother of one of them and another relative who got in touch with them, and I was informed about the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I return to the powerful figure who was obliged or who obliged, apparently, the local authorities to exchange these three. I want you to give the learned Judges your account of who the powerful figure was said to be and how you knew this, and there will, I think, come a time when you will seek from the Judges that the matter is dealt with in private session. When you reach that point, will you let us know. It may be immediately. Are you in a position in public session to identify, from what you were told, who the powerful influence was? Can you name that person in public session or do you wish to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that it was Mr. Milosevic, and we can discuss the details in another way if necessary. I would just like to add my thoughts or my question why, when the gentleman was so powerful, he didn't bring his influence to bear so that something should be done for other detainees all over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will go into private session with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the summary, paragraph 33 -- 43. The witness was transferred to the Kula camp on the 5th of July, 1993. There were some 80 to 100 prisoners there, all Muslims, brought from various camps in Bosnia, later to be joined by 67 Croats brought, detained but kept separately there in conditions as bad as at KP Dom, prisoners disappearing from Kula camp in different ways, some being taken to work at the front lines where they were seriously wounded or killed, the witness staying there for another year until his release. It doesn't seem to me necessary to give precise dates given that he is anonymous. And paragraph 44 is evidence to be given live, but again I shan't give too much detail. The Chamber will find at tab 3 and tab 4 certificates covering his detention, first of the Bosnian authorities and then of the ICRC if I've got it the right way round. The Bosnian authority certificate gives as date of detention, first detention, a date in April 1992. The ICRC gives a date of detention in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 1120, the last topic. Can you explain, please, that discrepancy? Don't give the precise dates in case they can be identifying of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. A characteristic trait of the Serb authorities was to manoeuvre with the dates, if I can put it that way, regarding the beginning of detention. I saw several such certificates when I left the camp. I first saw my own, which is incorrect regarding the date of my taking into custody. And I saw many other certificates where they concealed many months of detention for many detainees. When we intervened with the International Red Cross for the date to be corrected, they were not in a position to make any corrections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Actually, they told us, "You have the exact date with your authorities, and you will be giving your statements to your authorities and then that date will be taken as the correct date for the beginning of your detention."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The significance of the period between April and August 1992, identified to the ICRC by the detaining authorities as a period when you were not in detention, being what, in your judgement, Witness 1120?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: They simply wanted to present things falsely. They do not realise that in doing so, they unmasked themselves regarding the falsehoods that they bandied about later on. Regarding my particular case, which is quite striking, if the date of my captivity is mentioned, it is not logical, because on the 13th of that same month, there was virtually not a single Muslim left in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I ask. You will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Could you both remember, both yourself and the witness, please, to leave a pause after speaking; and could you, Witness B-1120, could you please keep an eye on the accused's microphone and make sure it's switched off before you answer. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin the cross-examination, Mr. May, I should like to ask you that for this witness and the following one I be given a little more time, because I have quite a lot of questions and a lot of material. Not too much more, but just a little more than you usually give for 92 bis witnesses, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1120, the investigators of Mr. Nice, you gave Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to them so far three statements: On the 19th and 20th of April, 1996; on the 20th of June, 1997; and the 20th of October, 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 15th of July, 1994, to authorised personnel of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say the centre for security for Sarajevo, you also gave a statement about the events that you have testified to and spoke to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind the chronology of this in which you gave statements, can you tell me this: Which of the statements represents the result of your best recollections? Or to be more precise, tell me which of those statements most completely reflects the events you're testifying about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I think that is the first statement, but there's no vital difference or difference in substance between that and the rest of the statements given to the representatives of the Tribunal. They were all -- the ones to the Tribunal focused on certain questions and issues, whereas my first statement took the chronology of events from when I was detained to when I was released, that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, is it true that as of May 1990, from the very inception, you were a member of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, testifying in another trial before this same Tribunal, you stated that you didn't have any important function within the SDA party. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, the one you gave to the investigators on the 20th of April, 1996, on page 2, paragraph 2, is it true that you said you were a member of the Main Board of the SDA of Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would the registrar come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So membership in the Main Board of the SDA party of Foca, you don't consider that to be an important function, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. I didn't speak publicly, I didn't change my relationship towards people as an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking whether you thought it was an important post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, look: You've both been told this. You've both been warned. We will not get on and this cross-examination will not continue unless the rules are followed. Now, it's difficult, I know, because you both speak the same language, but can you please bear this in mind and just look at his microphone. And, Mr. Milosevic, don't interrupt the witness, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll do my best, Mr. May, not to create any problems for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, your membership in the SDA party and the post you occupied means that as a member of that party and a member of the Main Board of that party for Foca, and as an intellectual yourself, you accepted the platform and programme orientation of that party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, but may I now say something with respect to the platform and programme of the party and my options and how I came to be a member of the party? Let me explain this to the Trial Chamber. I became a member of the said party at my own -- on the basis of my own positions after having studied the party programme carefully. I realised that the party programme was a good one in the sense that it advocated good neighbourly relations with the Serbs and Croats and that it wished to see equality prevail in all respects, that it also wanted to ensure everybody's equal social, national, and religious rights, and that drew me closer to it. In the second half of the programme of that mentioned party, it said, Mr. Milosevic, something that I was very happy to see and made me decide. What it said was that the SDA was in favour of a united Yugoslavia, a united currency, and united uniform foreign policy. One army, one police, and all it sought was the distribution of state organs, that they be deployed some of them in Ljubljana, Zagreb, Sarajevo, Belgrade, Ljubljana, et cetera, not all state organs to be headquartered in Belgrade. But that was the essential thing for me and which prevailed upon me to become a member of that party, namely that the party in its programme exclusively advocated the preservation of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, following on from your guidelines and cautions, I didn't want to interrupt the witness, but would you please bear in mind that it's his job to give answers to my questions and not to put forward any number of reasons for which he accepted the party programme. It takes up a lot of time. That's one thing, and it's superfluous on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but I think he was entitled to give that answer and to explain his position since you were asking him about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked him whether he accepted the platform and orientation of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does that mean that you were in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina's secession from the SFRY, that is to say, an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Milosevic, no. We're talking about 1990 when I became a member, that is to say, four or five parties -- months after the party had been established at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that was still the time when we all had in mind a united Yugoslavia, and we thought that it could and should be preserved as a single state, as one country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you said that among other things you were attracted to the party because it advocated equality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that 1.600.000 Serbs at the referendum held in 1991 voted to remain within the SFRY, that is to say, precisely those ideas that you were advocating?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm wondering if this political debate is taking us anywhere. This witness is giving evidence about what happened in Foca, and to extend the debate into a general discussion is simply irrelevant. Now, let us move on to Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we will of course return to Foca, but precisely because the witness said that he was in favour of equality and preserving Yugoslavia, I asked him whether he knew that 1.600.000 Serbs went to the referendum in 1991 and voted to remain in Yugoslavia. And on the other hand, the Muslims and Croats, those citizens, called for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can hear evidence about that in due course. He's told you what his position was. Just a moment. Please don't -- please don't interrupt. We will hear in due course, no doubt, other evidence about those matters, but what you should concentrate on is this witness's evidence and what happened in Foca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with Your Honour Judge May. If we were to summarise and make a precis dating back from 1991, we'll never get to the point and get to my answers, and I have answers for Mr. Milosevic. First of all, let me say that it's not true that in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Witness, you're here to answer questions. Now, I know you have views and no doubt feel strongly about these matters, but I must ask you just to answer the questions shortly as you can, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the centre of security on the 15th of July, 1994, and that's on page 1, paragraph 1, you said that the creation of this duality was a reservation among the population of Foca, that they became reserved. You speak about the way they drifted apart and this fact that they were reserved. Now, the vital question of staying on within the SFRY or the creation of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and a referendum, actually, the referendums that were held, was that the basis for this reserved attitude and the rift and duality that you mention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know that you, with the leaders from all the republics, held a number of consultations and meetings in an attempt to preserve Yugoslavia. You did not agree to any compromise which was put on the table, and you took a different course. The party system was dissolved, a multi-party system came into being, and according to the multi-party system, the Serbs saw that they could not enjoin the same rights they had enjoyed in the communist system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I don't think we can deal with this in this way. Mr. Witness, I must ask you to -- I know you're trying to answer the questions, but we cannot go into a political debate here about events all over Bosnia. Now, Mr. Milosevic, unless you've got questions about this witness's evidence, I'm going to bring the cross-examination to a close. Having a general debate about what happened in Bosnia with one particular witness from one municipality does not assist us and is not relevant. Now, have you any questions about the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's move on and focus on Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, is it true that the Party of Democratic Action in the summer of 1991 held a rally in Foca at which one 100.000 people took part approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. But no incidents broke out during the rally nor was anything said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you that. All I wanted to establish was that the meeting was attended by 100.000 people, because yesterday we had a witness here who claimed otherwise. Now, is it true that the Serbian Democratic Party later on also held a rally in Foca at the Suceska stadium with the attendance of approximately 10.000 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, it did hold a rally at that stadium that you mentioned but I don't know that there were just that number of people present. I think that there were far more people, but I never attended meetings of the SDS myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes. Then I take it that you don't really know although you are an inhabitant of Foca. Now, is it true that in the Foca region there were about 50.000 people living there roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 52 per cent roughly were Muslims and 48 per cent roughly Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, how do you explain the fact that at the rally of the SDS -- of the SDA in Foca there were five times more Muslims than were inhabitants of the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, people from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina came in to attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't this fact in itself -- don't you feel that this fact in itself represents, in addition to the various options for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, a clear threat made to the Serbs or, rather, the Serb people who wished to remaining living in a federal state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of my time restrictions, I'm not going to quote from the speeches delivered at that rally, but there will be occasion for me to do on -- in due course. Mr. 1120, in your statement of the 15th of July, 1994, on page 1, paragraph 2, you say that already after two or three sessions of the municipal parliament, the Assembly members of the SDS refused to accept the proposed agenda and, therefore, the work of the Assembly was paralysed. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, who proposed an agenda which the Serb Assembly members refused to accept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: The club of deputies of the SDS and the SDA. However, Mr. Milosevic, I should like to clarify a point here: The SDS only wanted to gain time in order to be able to arm itself properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. We didn't hear the beginning of that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was in their favour to gain time for the purpose that I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what has the agenda got to do with this? I have the feeling that the microphone isn't being switched on straight away. I'll wait to see the light come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That is because you are not pausing, despite numerous complaints. You're both not pausing. You'll get the microphone cut off if you don't. Now, there's no point going on if you don't follow the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, does that mean then that paralysis of the work of the local Assembly was due not to Serb non-cooperativeness but due to the fact that their positions were being ignored even though they represented half the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No, no. Their positions were not ignored. What was important was what I already said, and the important thing is that the Serbs, after the multi-party system was introduced, could not reconcile themselves to having as much power as is their due corresponding to the number of inhabitants and the number of votes, which is a basic principle of democracy, because in the previous system they enjoyed far greater rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I hope you will agree with me - the Serbian Democratic Party was opposed to the previous system and had a clearly anti-communist attitude.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I can't elaborate on that. It was certainly nonsense that it behaved in that way while it must -- it was aware that under the previous system the Serb people was dominant throughout at all levels, from the local level to the top state leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, wasn't a principle that was respected at all levels in Bosnia and Herzegovina to bear in mind the share of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims from the top to the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. I said that was the rule and it was in the programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is: Was that rule complied with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. The rules of the SDS were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't tie you with these facts now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it beyond doubt that within the SDA an aspiration was voiced for secession from the SFRY whereas the Serbs wanted to continue living in the same state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? What is the relevance of this as far as this witness is concerned? We're just wasting time and you're taking up your time. You've asked for more time. We'll have seriously to consider whether you should get it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'm asking this because the witness, in his statement of the 15th of July, claims, on page 1, paragraph 3, that the SDS members of parliament wanted a state of chaos and that this suited them. Surely chaos was needed by those who wanted to secede and not by those who wanted to preserve the state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I explain something to you, Mr. Milosevic? It has been explained before. It doesn't matter what is in the statements. You can use what is in the statements to contradict the witness, if you wish, or indeed you can ask questions about it, but what is in the statements is not evidence in this case. What's evidence is what the witness has given in evidence here or in his transcript. So the fact that something in the statement is there doesn't matter as far as this case is concerned. So whatever he said there is irrelevant unless he repeats it here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we didn't get the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to your Rule 92 bis, I don't have any oral statements of his but only the written statements and that's why I'm referring to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have the transcript. It's the transcript which is in the evidence in this case of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us speed things up, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are claiming that in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also in Foca the Serbs had intended to carry out an aggression against their own republic and their own people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: For their benefit and with the assistance of the JNA. They wanted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to conduct an aggression against their town, and they could never have been able to do it without the assistance of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. 1120. In the statement you gave the centre -- to the centre of the security services, you claim with emphasis that all members of the SDS participated in procuring and distributing weapons to the Serb population to Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true what you say in the next sentence, that the local Serbs were distributed weapons from the JNA warehouse in Filipovici? This is the warehouse close to Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I don't have such information that those weapons came only from that warehouse but from all the warehouses containing infantry weapons all over Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a general answer. I asked you specifically about what you say here. The JNA warehouse from Filipovici. How do you know that? Were you there? Did you see the Serbs being given weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Didn't I say that I saw weapons distributed from that warehouse. But, for instance, from the Lukavice warehouse near Sarajevo and other military facilities especially around Sarajevo, it is known with certainty that weapons were delivered to Serbs in trailer trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why then would members of the SDS from Foca, as you claimed in the statement I quoted from, took part in procuring weapons if, as you say, they were distributed to them from JNA warehouses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the warehouse which is 12 kilometres from Foca had only 12 JNA soldiers there and that the commander of this small unit was Muharem Kurtovic, a Muslim Major?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that the local Serbs could be given weapons by a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. I think in that warehouse there were virtually no weapons because it was a warehouse for other military equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to hear. So this was quite incorrect that weapons were distributed to anyone from that warehouse, and therefore, also to the SDS and the Serbs. Mr. B-1120, are you familiar with the statement of Muhamed Cengic, one of the leaders of the SDA for a newspaper called Liljan when he said that the Muslims of Foca long before the outbreak of the conflict in Foca had organised themselves militarily and that they even had armed night patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that fact true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know who Senad Sahinpasic, known as Sajo, is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I met him quite late but I never had any closer contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to my information, you did not agree with his extremist ideas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I couldn't call them extremist, but people often differ in opinions, and that is their right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he was an activist of the SDA with extremist views towards Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of his advocacy of a conflict with the Serbs and their expulsions from Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that is so, do you know at least that together with other extremists he distributed weapons to the local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. I do not know, sir, that the Muslim population was armed. If they had been armed like the Serbs, then the fighting in Foca would probably have lasted longer or maybe the war would have taken a different course. In four months, 21.000 Muslims would not have been expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, didn't you a moment ago confirm yourself that long before the outbreak of the conflict in Foca the Muslims were militarily organised and that they had night patrol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. You misunderstood me. You're inverting what I said. I said that they didn't have patrols, that they didn't have weapons, and that they were absolutely empty-handed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all that Cengic stated about Foca is untrue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: It's up to you to draw your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know anything about the organisation of barricades in Donje Polje, which is very close to the centre of Foca according to the witness we heard yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. I think that I was already in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: My answer? No. I think I was already detained then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in detention before the beginning of the conflict in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware of the date of my detention. I didn't move anywhere except from my apartment to my workplace, and I didn't know what exactly was going on in various parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself say that the conflicts in Foca started on the 6th or the 7th of -- as you say, but you were not in detention then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Let me clarify that. On the 8th of April, I left my apartment to go and do some shopping in a store close by. In front of that shop, an armed Serb was standing and several other Serbs, and he was explaining to them that that night the JNA centre and the post office had been taken control of, and these buildings were in the centre of town. I looked up at the JNA building, and I saw an armed soldier pointing his gun towards the street that was used by people and on which the armed Serb was standing, the one I knew. And at the entrance to the JNA cultural centre, I turned around and saw another three armed soldiers of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you yourself now said, you heard from them that the JNA cultural centre had been taken control of. How then can you claim that the JNA had taken part in the conflicts in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, you see that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw people in uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there were locals that I knew personally. But these other men who came to assist the Serbs from the former JNA, I didn't know them, but they were wearing the uniforms of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, please, who did the Serbs fight against in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: They simply expelled the population, because actually there couldn't have been any battles if one nation didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that this conflict that lasted ten days was one-sided and the Muslims did not fight the Serbs but the Serbs just came and took over Foca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Precisely so, with the assistance of the JNA and paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no exchange of artillery fire between Serb and Muslim forces? There was no exchange ever fire and that attack on Foca went on for ten days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Artillery shooting from the hills there was by Serb forces, and infantry weapons were used in town so as to intimidate the Muslim population and force them to flee, whereas the men were captured immediately and taken to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your fellow citizen Avdic explained yesterday that the Muslim side fired -- I'm not going to mention the number of shells that didn't explode, that didn't go off. He was telling us that. So were those shells fired or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know anything at all about the artillery positions of the Muslims in a part of town known as Sukovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Muslim positions existed also within the KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that there was fierce fighting on the edges of the Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: From what I learnt later, there was in the direction of Gorazde and Trnovo, there were some conflicts on the edges of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In view of the duration of the conflict in Foca, can we infer that the forces were quite balanced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No, far from it, because the town fell in such a short time. All that was needed was to cleanse the city, and that took that many days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. 1120, tell me, is it true that the first houses that were torched in Foca were Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that among the first to burn, if not the first, was the house of Milorad Kunarac, a maths teacher in the elementary school in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that later because I -- you mean Krnojelac, the mathematics teacher. You mentioned Kunarac. He himself told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that that house was in Donje Polje, where the Muslim forces had their strongest positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. It was more in the centre than in Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, do you have any idea as to how many Serb houses were torched during those conflicts in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge, but the gentleman that we mentioned told me that his house had been burnt. First it was his coffee bar in front of the house, and then the fire spread to his house too, which could have been caused by Serb forces, because they were opening fire at random all over town. Allow me to clarify: There was an order to all Serbs and Montenegrins to leave Foca in that critical period, and they had all moved to Montenegro with their families temporarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the first time I hear that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: This is very important, because that is why they moved so boldly forward, using infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't hear that. We didn't hear the beginning of the question. We didn't hear that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [redacted]. And let's go into private session for one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll avoid mentioning dates, the date of your detention, because I don't want it to be linked up with your -- with disclosing your identity at all. However, you say in your statements that on that particular date, the date you were arrested, you were arrested at your work post by the local Serbs wearing the old uniforms of the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Read that to the end, the rest of my statement. It says, "A JNA soldier came to the cellar and tied my hands and the hands of the other people there." That's what it says. An unknown individual as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what you said that you were arrested by the local Serbs wearing old JNA uniforms. That's what I was asking you about. And I'm asking you whether the fact that they were wearing old JNA uniforms, does that mean that they were members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as being the Serb territorials, and they held us for five or six hours until these others came who subsequently tied our hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were members of the local Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: The first ten or 12 held us there. Later on, JNA soldiers turned up as reinforcements to help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, you know full well that in Foca there were no JNA barracks and that the sole military facility was precisely the warehouse in Filipovici for which you yourself said that there were no weapons there but were used to stock fuel and some quartermaster supplies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: That's a good question, Mr. Milosevic. Up until then in Foca brigades and brigades could have arrived from the former JNA from all directions. So that's the crux of it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you claim that there were brigades and brigades coming in from all directions of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Up until that time they could have arrived, but they arrived in large numbers, two or three battalions, to help out the Serbs in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I have reliable information telling me that, and even the local Serbs in the contacts I had with them later on confirmed that, that they did come in to assist them. And the -- the soldiers from Serbia themselves said that they had come to help their Serb brethren in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say soldiers from Serbia, you mean paramilitary formations that were mentioned by the previous witnesses from Foca, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. But you know the uniforms that the JNA wore, and we know that the paramilitaries wore a uniform in their own particular style. I don't want to explain what the insignia was, the Eagles, the -- Seselj's men, Arkan's men, and so on and everything they had, but they were present there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just be specific, not to waste time. You didn't see a single JNA soldiers. You just heard of the presence of JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, as I said that during the night I was taken off to assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the one that took you off was a JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, there were two of them in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: May I just also explain my direct contacts with one of the JNA soldiers. On the third day or, rather, the third night upon arrival in the KP Dom, I was taken off to a solitary confinement cell by former JNA soldiers, soldiers of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that there were JNA soldiers in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. They had come to help out, and they stayed there for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now we can move on. We've arrived at the KP Dom. You are in detention there and prior to that, several days before that in the empty hangars of the Territorial Defence. That's where you were detained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that all those guards of the KP Dom, without exception, were local Serbs? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: For the first few days, there were both. Later on this was taken over. The command was taken over and direct contact with the detainees was assumed by the local guards, the ones that were there previously. And they would just bring in from time to time and throw detained civilians into the rooms. This was done by the JNA soldiers and the paramilitaries I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this, please, Mr. B-1120, the conflicts in Foca, were they in fact conflicts between the local inhabitants, Serbs on the one side and Muslims on the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. I don't think we can speak of a conflict. You can see that it was ethnic cleansing actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, I see. Ethnic cleansing you said. I didn't hear you properly, so I had to look at what you said on the transcript. Tell me, please, do you happen to know how many armed members of the Muslim formations withdrew from Foca after this fighting that went on for about ten days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know anything about their withdrawal towards Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: All I know is that after the town of Foca, the Serb forces advanced towards Ustikolina, the other large town, and that Ustikolina fell on the 26th. And they also went by the place mentioned, Filipovici. There was a barracks there in Ustikolina itself, actually, and that's where there were some soldiers. I don't know how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true and correct, Mr. 1120, that in your statement given to the security centre of Sarajevo, on page 11, paragraph 5, that you said that from the work platoon, from the members of the work platoon, you learnt that during the period from April 1992 to 1993, in the fighting in the Foca area, about 1.100 Serbs were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. That's what somebody from the work platoon said. But we can put a question mark after that. But I did mention it in my statement because that's what he said. And it was the individual whom I mentioned said this. However, what -- that was a year after the war, actually, and they probably meant the number of Serb losses on all the battlefronts around Foca, that is to say where they were advancing towards Gorazde and Trnovo, et cetera, because there were a lot of battles fought around Trnovo at that time there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1120, you're talking about the Foca area. Now, Foca is a municipality with 50.000 inhabitants, and we took note of that fact earlier on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that 1.100 Serbs were killed in those battles, can you truly claim that the Muslims were unarmed on the other side and that most probably these Serbs killed themselves in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, there were occasions where they killed themselves too, and that a lot of them died in battle, that is certain too. And the only route for the Muslims to get their resources was from war booty from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can take that to be an observation as well in your testimony, that this 1.100 killed Serbs, for the most part, died because they had killed themselves, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I've already given my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean if such a large number died or were killed on one side, in this particular case the Serb side, does that mean that the fighting in Foca and the surrounding parts went on for quite a long time? Actually, they never ceased. They never stopped throughout that whole year, from April one year to April the next year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Along the edges towards Gorazde quite certainly the fighting did go on for longer, and up towards Trnovo as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about the Muslim formations and their fighting and participation in the area in which you yourself say that 1.100 Serbs lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, it would emerge, Mr. Milosevic, that the Muslims became consolidated, consolidated their ranks in one way or another after a year had gone by, one year later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. B-1120, what does that mean, up until then, the conflict broke out on the 6th or 7th of April, as you yourself say, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fighting for Foca went on for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on, this fighting expanded to the broader area around Foca, and from your own information and facts, I take this figure of 1.100 Serbs killed - I'm using the figure you quoted - but many more were killed. So do you know anything about those Muslim formations, the ones which fought and were active in the region of Foca that you're testifying about, or don't you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how big the formations were or how they were organised. I don't know anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at least who was in command of those formations on the territory of the Foca region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1120. I'm going to just ask you one or two more questions, and here they are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that this was not in private session, what the witness claimed earlier on with respect to the name of a man whom he said was my business friend. Was that in private session or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The name was given in open session. The detailed mechanism whereby that information was available was given in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be sensible to go into private session, then, to have this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in public session now, so I would just like to cover a few more questions, because I saw from your testimony that you spoke about some Muslims fleeing to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What really happened? You mentioned that some people went looking for them, intervening, that they should be returned, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I think that we shouldn't go back to that matter, that in the summary everything was stated explicitly. All I can do is repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If all you can do is repeat, repeat. But if the accused has any questions, he's entitled to ask them. Now, what specifically is it that you want to ask, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. 1120, that in Serbia alone there were 70.000 Muslim refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Look, the witness can't deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I noted down here that President Bulatovic personally intervened for these 21 persons to be returned to the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the group consisted of 21?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, that group. But later on from the Montenegrin literal, more Muslim refugees were brought from Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, do you know how many thousand Muslim refugees there were in Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at least that there were several thousand of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milosevic, it is quite clear here that the Serb authorities or, rather, the political leadership of the SDS that I mentioned, went there, caught those people, and ordered that other Muslims be caught and captured and that Montenegrin politicians did this, rounding up the group from Uzin to Herceg-Novi, which automatically is indicative of the participation of Montenegro in the persecution of Muslims and their detention in camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. 1120. Do you know that in those days Yugoslavia was still operational, it still existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, but a Rump Yugoslavia. Actually, that is why we are mentioning this, Montenegro and Serbia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it logical if several thousand Muslims had fled to Montenegro, and the authorities in this particular case, the authorities from Foca, are asking from the authorities Niksic, Podgorica, or Uzin to arrest those 21 men who are suspected of criminal activity, that it is logical for them to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I'm sorry, criminal activity is not mentioned anywhere. You're just bringing this up as a thesis on your part. They are civilians who fled to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, and on the basis of which criteria were those 21 of them arrested when several thousand of them had fled to Montenegro and nobody treated them badly over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I don't think that was so. They were just transiting through Montenegro, going towards Sandzak and Macedonia. I -- it is not true that that many of them were kept in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where is Sandzak? Is Sandzak in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, of course Sandzak is in Serbia, but it's not in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Partially in Montenegro as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, yes, partially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone mistreat those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, the police that arrested those 21 people. First they were shut up in the police stations of the mentioned municipalities of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what has President Bulatovic got to do with the cooperation between the police of, for instance, Foca and Podgorica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Of course he has as being the most responsible leader of the Montenegrin people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the president of the Republic of Montenegro went into this matter as to whether a person looked for by the organs of the neighbouring republic would be given to those authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: In wartime and in the situation we are talking about, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what are you saying that President Bulatovic had anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Because the man I mentioned told me that and I know him well as he worked in the same institution as I did. I can also mention the names of those 21 people and others. Let me add that out of those 21, two died later on in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is certainly a tragedy that they died, but you haven't answered my question. What has President Bulatovic got to do with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, you know yourself. I don't want to elaborate that any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1120. If we're talking about camps and about the allegations of the leadership of Republika Srpska that there were no camps, do you remember that Radovan Karadzic wrote in public and through the media to Paddy Ashdown, who is now in Bosnia-Herzegovina, denying allegations that there were claims and inviting him to come and see for himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, and that is not true. Why was the International Red Cross not allowed to come to the camps and to register the detainees before?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had the information that the International Red Cross had access to all prisoners -- prisons or sentence for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness can't possibly know about your state of knowledge or what reports you received. All he can do is say what happened to him, which he has done, and give evidence about the conditions in the facility that he was in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're saying, Mr. May. I am just saying that these were public communications, and the witness must have been familiar with them. But let us leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to address another point. Mr. 1120, you said that -- that you were tied and escorted to a hangar or whatever by a JNA member. Tell me, on the basis of what did you come to the conclusion that he was a JNA member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: On the basis of his dialect, the accent he used, and the uniform he wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about the uniform, do you know that yesterday that a Muslim witness sitting in that same chair said that he too had that same kind of uniform in his home, because all military conscripts in those days or at least the majority of them had JNA uniforms in their apartments, and he's a man from Foca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: That is not true that that is what he said. He said, just I did -- he said, "When I was a military conscript, I wore that uniform." He didn't say that he had it at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not important for us to establish that with you, because there's a transcript from yesterday's proceedings. Is there anything else aside from the uniform on the basis of which you came to the conclusion that he was a JNA member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I think I told you enough. His accent and certain -- the way he behaved, because in that critical period, the Serbs moved away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, other witnesses have said and you too I think mentioned paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. I think they participated in the overall persecution of Muslims from and expulsion of Muslims from Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this man who tied you, could he have been a member of a paramilitary unit and not the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: It is more probable that he was a JNA member than a member of the paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no proof of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I've explained it to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. 1120. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B-1120, could you please provide some more explanations to Their Honours in connection only with your arrest and what you experienced while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: I think that is quite unnecessary for me to repeat. I don't know the umpteenth time that has been said and written for four or five times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness B-1120. You're a witness here. Now, you must answer the questions, if they're proper questions. If they're not, counsel will be stopped. As a witness, your duty is to answer the questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, but I was thinking of the time we have, and we don't wish to waste each other's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite clear that I was captured on the 11th of April at my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, allow me to put the question to you. From the moment you were arrested until you were exchanged, were you permanently under the control of other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now my question is the following: Those men who deprived you of your freedom, did they that they were members of the Serbian Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: At first, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you knew most of them because you were in contact with them and their families as part of your work? I won't mention what that work was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that they were under the command of Cicmil, I think his name was Milenko, and that he said that he was the commander and that he said that he was carrying out the orders of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that among them was Mladen Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew him too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Zecevic had a M-48 rifle that belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you cannot recollect some names of Serbs who were there but that you would recognise them if you saw then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. When I was giving my statement, I couldn't remember all 11 first and last names, but I knew them at the time they entered the institution to arrest me and the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. They were all local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes, local Serbs until darkness fell, and these three JNA soldiers arrived to tie our hands up and to take us away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must say that you didn't mention that in your first statements, but that doesn't matter. What matters is what you say here. Is it true that after that you were taken to Livade and shut up in the hangars of the Territorial Defence which used to contain equipment of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the time, there were no representatives of the JNA in the hangars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: That night, no. But as from the next morning, that is the 12th of April, they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't mention that earlier on. Okay. But what you say now matters. When you were in the KP Dom where you spent the amount of time you said, the guards worked in shifts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were normal police guards who used to work in the KP Dom before the war too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes they wore camouflage uniforms and sometimes former uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The military police only came to the administrative building, and they always wore camouflage uniforms."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes. But during the first few days, the military policemen did enter of the rooms of the detainees, searched them, seized weapons and other valuables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. "But I recognise some local Serbs that I recognised. For instance, Dragan Zelenovic. I don't know who was his superior, Krnojelac or the military police." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more point and then I'll close. Is it true that you never saw anyone being killed in the KP Dom? You describe that people died for the reasons you gave, but you never saw anybody being killed in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Not in the actual compound that we could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question. You knew that people were thrown into the nearby river.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: People on the higher stories of the KP Dom saw people being take he out of their rooms during the night between the 13th and the 13th of June, because it is very important because 35 men were taken out in that period, first in the administrative building, actually a room meant for mistreatment and torture of prisoners. They were first mistreated, beaten up, and then taken out outside when shots could be heard, and after that, the sound of something falling into the water from a height.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question is: Is what you said in your first statement true, that prisoners heard something being thrown into the river? "When I got in touch with those prisoners from the top floors, they told me what they heard, and we came to the conclusion that bodies were thrown into the river."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is some ambiguity in your answers as recorded on the transcript about the arming of Muslims in advance of the war. Was there any arming on an organised basis by the Muslims before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just spoken of the police taking arms from people once they were detained. What sort of arms were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Hunting weapons and the ones that they could procure legally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been asked about the detention generally. Was any reason -- and you gave an answer about ethnic cleansing. Was any reason given to you or, to your knowledge, to your fellow detainees to justify your being detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. What was stressed was that the SDA was to blame for that. But thousands and thousands of detainees never wanted nor were they members of the SDA party, and therefore that speaks of the fact that there was another plan, and that was the persecution and ethnic cleansing in the ways that have already been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of the person who took you into detention being more probably JNA than paramilitary. You've already given evidence of what you saw by way of uniform. Is there anything else you want to say that justifies your conclusion more probably JNA than paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: Well, I can't be more explicit but to say that there was a different sort of behaviour and the different -- a different uniform that he wore, and the accent, the accent that could be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Last question: The Cengic exchange, which you say was probably in January 1993, the accused has suggested that in the letter from the Cengics or on their behalf reference was to their being subject only to a blockade rather than to his being informed that they were in a camp. Do you know one way or another what was in the letter that was sent on the Cengics' behalf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1120
utterances.text: No. No, I really don't know of the contents of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction, Mr. May, if I may be allowed to make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the correction?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a question of an exchange of any kind. It was help to these people, not an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We hear that. Witness B-1120, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go, but just wait a moment while we let the blinds down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome will deal with the next matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
