utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is C-1171, and Mr. McKeon will take this witness. He is on his way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he's sitting outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could make a few remarks regarding the evidence regarding the Foca municipality. Pursuant to the Chamber's oral ruling of the 8th of May and its written decision of the 30th of June of this year, the transcripts and related exhibits of six witnesses were admitted without cross-examination. At this time I would seek to tender packages for those six witnesses to conclude the presentation of the Foca evidence. The first package would be for Witness B-1121. I would ask that all those exhibits be under seal as they were tendered under seal in the last proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us physically decide how we're going to do this. Yes. It looks like quite a lot coming up. It may be, rather than hand them over now, if we identify them and give them numbers now and then they can be handed in to us, it may be, later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. So would you go through the witnesses and we'll get exhibit numbers each time. We'll hand them over later, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that's B-1121, a binder of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. These are the Foca transcript witnesses 92 bis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-1537.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And all of those exhibits under seal. Witness B-1538, all of these exhibits under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1540, only tab 1 of that exhibit needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to witness B-1543, tabs 1 through 7 of that exhibit should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, B-1542, all of those exhibits should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. I'm just going to check with the Registry to make sure that they have everything and anything else they need. I gather that's all right. Anything else? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a final comment, Your Honour: There were two witnesses, B-1015 and B-1618, for which the Prosecution applied to have their transcripts admitted under 92 bis (D) and the Chamber ruled that they were required to appear for cross-examination. With respect to Prosecution witness B-1015, we are unable to locate this witness, and after extensive efforts, do not believe we will be able to locate this witness. We do not believe the witness's evidence is critical enough to warrant an application under 92 bis (C) and therefore we are withdrawing our 92 bis application with respect to that witness. That's 1015. With respect to B-1618, given the significant constraints on time, the Prosecution has reassessed this witness's contribution to the evidence in light of the other Foca evidence that has been introduced, and at this time would move to withdraw its application under 92 bis (D). We, of course, apologise for burdening the Court with consideration of that witness's matter. In fairness to the accused, if there is some evidence available from that witness that he would seek to introduce on the Defence case, we would, of course, cooperate in the production of that witness for the Defence case. And that concludes all of the evidence in the Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We'll go on with the next witness. Can we have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. Take the declaration, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. McKeon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I think as you know, you've been granted certain protective measures by the Trial Chamber, so I will refer to you by your pseudonym, C-1171, during the course of your testimony this morning. I would ask you if you could take a look at a piece of paper that's going to be shown to you and tell us, please, just by answering yes or no whether that's your name on the first line of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you previously testify here at the Tribunal in the case of Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday, did you have a chance to review a transcript of your testimony in English with the assistance of a language interpreter where you thought it necessary to help you with the English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of that review did you find a few errors in your transcript that you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask if a copy of the transcript could be placed in front of the witness and ask you to turn, please, first to page 952, line 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do that, it should have an exhibit number if it hasn't already got one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is tab 3 in the exhibits tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but what's the bundle?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P499.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have that in front of you, page 952, line 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- thank you. And there should the correct word be Transjug Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to page 955, lines 4 to 5 where it refers there to the Assembly of People's Guards, is that also known as the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 960, lines 4 through 8, please. There it says that you returned and stayed with your parents in September, and in fact, you stayed with your parents until September and then returned to their house in November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could turn to page 977, please, lines 15 through 18. You will see there you've described a big man in an olive-grey or green uniform of the former JNA without any insignia rank and you say he was a very big man, he wore a moustache, and he had a whistle. In fact, you were describing there, were you not, two different people that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, please, what the first man looked like and what the second man looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: The first man looked like this: He had a powerful body. He had a red beard and a cap, a brown cap, a woollen one, and he had maybe not a regular military uniform but a sort of strange kind of camouflage uniform. And the other one had a military uniform, and that one had a whistle, and he was most probably a commander in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see any insignia rank on the second man, and if so, why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No, because it was a windjammer of the former JNA, and there was no rank insignia. Probably the rank insignia was somewhere on the clothing underneath, on the shirt or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very grateful to you if you would kindly ask the witness to speak up, because despite the fact that I have the headset in my ear, I can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you went a bit closer to the microphone that might help. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally could you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Finally, could you turn, please, to page 981, line 12 of the transcript of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will see in the middle or to the end of that line there is the a name that starts Zambata, Z-a-m-b-a-t-a -- in fact the correct name should be, first name should be Slaven, S-l-a-v-e-n, surname Vukojevic, V-u-k-o-j-e-v-i-c, and this person is also known as Zambata; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: With these corrections, Your Honour, we would like to offer the transcript of this witness's testimony into evidence under Rule 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: This is a summary of the witness's previous testimony, Your Honour. This man is a man from Vukovar, Croatia. During the summer of 1991 when the shelling of Vukovar started, the witness joined in the defence of Vukovar. By about the 16th of November, 1991, it was obvious to the witness that it would be impossible for them to defend the city any longer. On the 18th of November, 1991, the witness went with his parents to the Vukovar Hospital because he heard there was going to be an evacuation convoy from there. He registered at the hospital on the list of wounded upon his father's insistence because he had been wounded several times. The witness saw military or paramilitary forces come to the hospital from the city centre, specifically a Major of the JNA in an armoured vehicle with several members of his unit. They entered the hospital ground, and the major established the security at the facility. The witness spent the night at the hospital. The next morning, the witness was called out of the hospital with shouts and was forced through the emergency door of the hospital. The witness and others were lined up in two rose and searched. There were three buses waiting guarding by soldiers carrying machine-guns. After the buses were loaded, the buses went to the JNA barracks. There, the convoy of the three buses formed a semicircle in the middle of the compound. Within the compound were quite a number of people that were circling the buses, some of them shouting, some of them making threats. After some time, another two or three buses joined the others waiting there. They stayed there for quite some time, listening to curses, threats, and insults. After about two hours, the buses left the JNA barracks base and went to Ovcara. At Ovcara, the passengers from the buses were disembarked one by one. Everything was taken away from these people, everything of value. People were forced to pile up their personal belongings on a large heap. The people were then taken into the hangar itself where they had to run a gauntlet. The people in the gauntlet who were there to meet them were beating them with all sorts of things they had in their hands, including shovels and iron bars. Inside the hangar, the torture continued. The witness himself was hit on the head, probably with an iron bar. As he ran the gauntlet he was hit several times, and then he was thrown on the straw that was in the hangar. The people doing the beatings were wearing different clothes, some with the insignia of the JNA. After the buses had been emptied, the witness estimates that there were between 200 and 300 people in the building. One soldier, neat and tidy in a camouflage uniform, was making a list of detainees. Inside the building was a man in a JNA uniform. He used a whistle to channel the activities of the others and he would stop them or tell them to continue. Inside the hangar, the terror continued. Ten to 20 people were going around in circles, questioning first one person and then another, and torturing them and beating them using all the resources they had available, including rifles, baseball bats, wooden sticks, hands, arms, feet, legs, and military boots. One person was beaten so badly the witness is convinced this person died from his injuries. He saw them kicking this person, beating him with weapons, and stamping on his head and body. They made this person sing Chetnik songs. The witness saw another man beaten with his own crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After night fell, people were led outside in groups of ten or 15. They were ordered to line up by the soldiers. This happened about every ten or 15 minutes. People were selected according to their position inside the hangar, starting from the door. The witness himself was selected in the third, fourth, or fifth group. He was taken out and put on a military vehicle with a canvas cover. There were approximately ten or 15 people in his group. They were told they were being transferred to another hangar. During the journey, the witness saw an opportunity and jumped from the truck. He ran as fast as he could in the direction of Vukovar. Shortly after he jumped, he heard a short burst of fire and a couple of individual shots and that was the last he heard. He was recaptured shortly thereafter, beaten, and then taken to Stari Jankovci under guard. There he was beaten again. He was eventually taken to Sid and then Sremska Mitrovica, and finally ended up in a prison in Belgrade. In Sid, the witness was asked by his interrogator what he knew about Ovcara and how many people had been killed there or whether anyone had been killed. The witness was eventually charged in Belgrade with the crime of armed revolt and crime against a civilian population but the trial was never completed. The witness was released from military prison on 14 August 1992 as part of a prisoner exchange. And I have just a couple of additional questions, Your Honour, that's not from his transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were at Sremska Mitrovica, were you ever held in a cell in the basement called "the ice room"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why this was called "the ice room"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Probably because of the cold that was in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided in this room with anything to keep you warm while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Nothing special except an old army blanket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, while you were in this room, did you ever hear noises of other prisoners being beaten? And if so, could you tell the Trial Chamber what you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, you could hear the blows, the screams, and the fact that people were being mistreated. I couldn't see anything because we were in a closed-off space, but I heard the sound, the noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, during your time at Sremska Mitrovica, were you yourself ever beaten and did you suffer any injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: They did beat me upon arrival when they took me to Mitrovica, and while I was taken for interrogation I would receive blows. I was beaten a little more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the war in Vukovar, did you ever have the opportunity to visit Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try again. During the war, before the fall of Vukovar, did you ever have the opportunity to go over to Vukovar Hospital for any reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: At all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your purpose for going over to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: There was some wounded men in our unit, so we would frequently go there to visit them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital, were you allowed to enter the hospital carrying a gun? And if so, what did you have to do with your weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Nobody was allowed to enter the hospital with weapons on them. There were guards which -- which stood at the entrance to the hospital, and each of us had to leave our weapons before entering the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Finally, I'd like to have placed in front of the witness tab 2 from the exhibits. This is the annex from the Croatia indictment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, did you have the opportunity to take this list and mark it with a pink marker, indicating people that you saw on the 19th or 20th of November at either the Vukovar Hospital, on the buses, at the JNA barracks, at Ovcara, or on the truck itself from which you jumped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all the questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1171, your testimony relates to the year 1991, the whole of it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it beyond dispute that Croatia, in those days, the days you're testifying about, was certainly a component part of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No, it is not beyond dispute. As of 1990, Croatia was a formed state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the earliest recognitions of independence occurred in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That is your opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are facts, but you don't know consider it to have been a component part of the SFRY in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: It probably was, but not in the way you probably think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't qualify. Anyway, in those days, in fact, the president of the Presidency was Stjepan Mesic from Croatia, et cetera, et cetera. So in 1991 it certainly was a component part of the SFRY. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Conditionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Reading your statement to the investigators on the 14th of July, 1995, I see that the -- at the end of the summer 1991, in the summer of 1991, you joined units of the National Guards Corps in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It true that you were under the direct command of Mile Dedakovic, known as Jastreb, the hawk, and Branko Borkovic, known as the small hawk or Mali Jastreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I know they are not from Vukovar, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that they were sent there from Zagreb to form armed units in Vukovar, the aim of which first to expel as many Serbs as possible from Vukovar and then to engage in combat activity against the JNA and its members. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did you join them as soon as they arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they arrive? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that. And is it true that in those days the town mayor of Vukovar was Marin Vidic, Bili?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was commissioner of the government for Vukovar, not the town mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Croatia for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, the commissioner of the government of Croatia for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that before the Jastrebs and Borkovic came to the territory of Vukovar there were organised and well-armed units there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that. Have you ever heard of Ferdinand Jukic known as Jejo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that already at the beginning of the summer of 1991 large quantities of various weapons were reaching Vukovar organised precisely by those Jukic known as Jejo, and a local policeman called Vladimir Majo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that purchases of these weapons were financed by the Ministry of Defence of the Croatia, the weapons you had at your disposal in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that Jastreb immediately after forming -- arriving in Vukovar formed companies and a brigade from Borovo Naselje of the ZNG, headed by -- and a brigade from Mitnica with Ivas Soljic, a brigade for Sajmiste headed by Stipe Susic and an operative brigade headed by Ivica Arbanas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of these formations were you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: In the National Guards Corps, which later became the Croatian army and the 204th brigade. These were four brigades of the ZNG, which one were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of this structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Jastreb, both the older one and the younger one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Jastreb, just Jastreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of Danijel Rehak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he select members of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: He took part in the formation of the Croatian army or at least the National Guards Corps when I was involved in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you yourself say, you were a commander of a unit for placing mines in Vukovar and the surroundings, which was under the direct control of Jastreb and Borkovic as you now say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, because Danijel Rehak participated together with Borkovic in forming that brigade of the national guards, that is the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had between eight and ten people on an average in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Let's say that that was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in September 1991, under instructions of Marin Vidic, Borkovic formed a police unit, a military police unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: A military police unit existed. How and who formed it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that beginning with the 3rd of September, 1991, a JNA garrison in Vukovar was blocked in terms of water and electricity supplies, the PTT lines, as well as supplies of food to the soldiers in the garrison could not be delivered as of the 3rd of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't part of the defence forces then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please speak up, because I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was not in the defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: From the media yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that already during the summer of 1991 this man with his legionnaires set up rocket systems at Count Erceg's palace used for constant attacks against the JNA and its units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that. Very well. And within the National Guards Corps in Vukovar was is there any other mine unit except yours, the one you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Formally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Tell me, please, Mr. 1171, are you known by a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: You mean a wartime nickname, a nom de guerre?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [redacted]. We'll go back into private session if you have any more question about this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, let us not go into private session. I will not repeat this nickname, but I will ask the witness questions bearing that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. 1171, why did you not tell the investigators that you were known under that nickname during the period you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I did not omit anything that was important for any kind of investigation or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here a report of the Permanent Mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva in which, on a page bearing your ERN number 00074372, says: The charges are, and then three persons are named including yourself, your first and last name and nickname, the one we've just established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we'll just take this in private session. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing that wasn't in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it true that these two persons were arrested in Vukovar in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, in the surrounding parts of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were together in the military prison; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. We were detainees in the military prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't quite clear on one point when you answered a question from Mr. McKeon. You were talking about some abuse, mistreatment, serious mistreatment. I would like you to be specific in your answer to this. In the military prison in Belgrade, did anybody mistreat you, abuse you in any way, or subject you to any kind of torture? So I'm asking you about the military prison in Belgrade now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No. At the military prison, nobody mistreated me or physically abused me at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you all give statements to the military investigating organs in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I gave a statement in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it also true that you were not an expert only for the devices that we mentioned earlier on but also for other types of weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, tell me what you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in addition to the devices that you handled that we mentioned a moment ago, these lethal devices, that you had knowledge of other types of weapons as well? Can you explain what an Osa is when it comes to weapons? What kind of a weapon is Osa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I can only say in principle. It is an anti-armoured device, anti-armoured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At you personally, Mr. 1171, did anybody shoot at you personally from a catering establishment in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: At me? I don't know. Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that you, yourself, when shooting from this weapon, this Osa weapon at the end of October 1991, completely destroyed the catering establishment - a catering establishment, I don't want to mention its name - and already the next day you did the same, shooting at another catering establishment, both of them in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. It's alleged, Witness 1171, that you destroyed a catering establishment using a particular weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's nonsense. I never had any weapon like that for me to use it for any purpose, even military purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wish to remind you, in this same document, and I'm not going to mention the name at all, it's your first and last name - the name of the page is 00074371, the ERN number - and it says -- it gives your name and surname, "from Vukovar, member of the Croatian National Guard -- a civilian from Vukovar, member of the Croatian National Guard, charged for the war crime against the civilian population under Article 142, paragraph 2, in connection with paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. [In English] At the end of October 1992 in violation of the norms of international law relating to armed conflicts, he hit unprotected civilian facilities by firing a missile from an Osa missile-launcher at --" [Interpretation] And then it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about what it says. The witness says he has never fired one. So he simply denies it, so there's no point putting it again. The fact that it's written down doesn't make it any truer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is an official report, and I hope that you will exhibit it, and you might be interested in reading it, Mr. May. If you refuse to do so, then that's your affair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic identifies me as a civilian. I wasn't a civilian. So there's a misunderstanding there. I was militarily organised, and my actions were military, not as a civilian from the region. So there seems to be some mix-up there, basic mix-up. And as I say, I never used that kind of weapon at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just read what it says here. I'm not giving any qualifications about you at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: All right, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, are you going to accept this document or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit it for what it's worth, yes. Give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. 1171, as you claim that you did not destroy these civilian facilities, do you know at all that those particular facilities were in fact destroyed, as were the facilities of local Serbs, using those kind of devices in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Did you say that was October, or what month?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've just handed it over to the registrar of this Trial Chamber, so I don't know exactly. I can't say, but I can find it, of course. It's October 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That was wartime activity. So there's no sense in speaking about that terrible shelling, that somebody blew up somebody's facilities when your forces ignited the whole town, which you can't deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come to adjourn. We are going to adjourn now, Witness C-1171, for 20 minutes. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibit which has just been handed in, 161, D161, is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one point. Over the break, I had a chance to look at D161, and I wanted to bring to the Court's attention that the second incident describes with an Osa missile launcher, in fact, it's somebody else's name that is above that. It is not the name of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, we have to adjourn at half past one today, which means we've got a little over three-quarters of an hour. We will divide the time as best we can. Mr. Milosevic, you've had half an hour. If you can finish in the next half hour, we'll perhaps give you another five minutes or so. We must give enough time for the amicus, very briefly, and for the re-examination, but we must finish at half past one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Mr. May, to get through this as quickly as possible, the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said, Mr. 1171, that you were not a paramilitary formation and to the investigators on the 14th of June, 1995, in your statement on page 3, paragraph 1, you said the following, referring to your group, the group that we mentioned, you say, I don't want to say its name and you say and I quote: "We were not a paramilitary unit." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, I can't see the document, but that's how it was. We really weren't a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what law it was, republican or federal, dating back to 1991 provided for this unit or the Croatian National Guards Corps as a legal armed formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that kind of document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I didn't have the documents. I can't tell you the number of the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 1, you claim that you were an ordinary citizen and that as such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of his statement so he can follow. Has he got one? Perhaps the usher could help him. I don't know if he can find his way around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I was saying, page 3, paragraph 1, you claim that you were an ordinary citizen, citizens who tried to defend their homes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Of course that's what we did. We were militarily organised citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who attacked you, for example, in March 1991? Who was it that attacked you and which Dom in Vukovar was threaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I'm talking about my inclusion into the conflict, not about all the conflicts that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1171. Now, do you know who the Croat from Vukovar is by the name of Zvonimir Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Never heard of him. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell me whether you know anything about this other man or, rather, what he is saying, what he says, because you had contacts with Glavas and Mercep, and otherwise it's the statement of Zvonimir Ostojic which was handed over to me by Mr. McKeon. 0263353 is the ERN number. That's the first page. And it says: "The positions of Glavas and Mercep which I heard on several occasions were the struggle to establish the independent State of Croatia which it would include parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that on these territories the problem of the Serbs should be solved in such a way as killing a third, changing the religion of the third and expelling the remaining third." Do you know of those positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I never had anything to do with those two men, so I really can't comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know their attitudes and positions that were common knowledge in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I didn't know of those positions, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the other thing that he says: When it comes to military organisation, I know that Mercep and Zadro, Blago Zadro were the main people in the Vukovar municipality who were to organise an armed resistance against the JNA and that there was a Crisis Staff for Vukovar made up of Mercep Tomislav, Zadro Blago, Gazo Josip, Radas S., and another one or two persons who were just there as figure heard whereas the mainstay was being held by Mercep and Zadar. Wasn't that how it was, Mr. 1171?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't know anything of that. I didn't take part in any of it nor was I included in any of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a statement, Mr. May, which was served on me by Mr. McKeon's side, and I think it can be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1171, on page 3 of your statement, you say that around the 16th, 1991 is the year, with the intention of joining the convoy and fleeing from Vukovar, you went to the Vukovar Hospital and found a lot of people there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite right, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how was it? What is right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: What is right is that when the defence was disbanded or, rather, when Jastreb left the headquarters and command post, I disbanded my soldiers and went back home. And then rumours started going round that some sort of evacuation was being organised and that everybody should gather round in the hospital compound. So that is closer to the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to quote paragraph 5 on page 3 of the B/C/S version, the Serbo-Croatian version of your statement: "I heard over the radio that there might be a convoy which would be taking people elsewhere in Croatia from the town so with my parents I went to the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th of November where I found many people, but nowhere was the convoy to be seen. My father told that I should go to the hospital and put my name down on the list of injured in the hospital."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was a little different from what you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a little different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depends how this was interpreted or translated. I can't see my own handwriting. But even if that's what it says, I didn't go to the hospital to put my name down as somebody who had been wounded, and I didn't listen to the radio. I didn't even have a radio set. So that wasn't how I reached this piece of information. I don't know how this was interpreted. Now, when we got there, people began saying that a list of wounded persons for evacuation purposes was being formed, and as I had been wounded on several occasions, my name was entered onto that list, and my father prevailed upon me to do so, to come forward.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you, Mr. May, to return that original to me, please, but I have here an original book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there were many people in the Vukovar Hospital, and I have the original logbook from the -- or register from the Vukovar Hospital, and in it we have an entry of the 2nd of November, 1991, going up to the 18th. The number is 610 -- from 610 to 655 are the numbers listed, which makes a total of 45 persons during all those difficult 18 days of fighting in Vukovar, in the hospital, according to this hospital logbook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, that must be some kind of forgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can take a look at the book. It is the original copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. May, you can have a look at it. I've marked the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A paper clip denotes the pages referring to that critical time, from the beginning to the 18th of November. And you can see the numbers, the persons admitted throughout that time, and the total number is 45 persons, and the numbers range from 610 to 655.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say. I've never had figures of this kind before my eyes, and this is the first time that I'm -- I've been given a chance to look at this kind of document. Without questioning its authenticity - I don't want to enter into that, whether this has been certified and proclaimed original - I don't understand your question, and what has that got to do with my overall testimony at all?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has to do with your assertion saying that the hospital was full of wounded people, whereas there we can see that only 45 persons were admitted during those 18 days, from the beginning of November up until the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. And what about the others that were admitted throughout the war and it lasted longer than the 2nd of November onwards?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. 1171, that in actual fact you, just like the other members of the Croatian National Guards Corps in fact filled the hospital up with -- you presented yourselves as being falsely wounded so that you could join a convoy with people who were actually wounded to leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That is a pure insinuation on your part, and it is not correct either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, will you please accept this book and exhibit it, but can I have the original back, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We can't do all this together. Let us begin -- we'll have a look at the book, if we may. Now, the only way we can exhibit it is by having it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I'm producing it and offering it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. And the Prosecution too must be able to have a look at it. You can have it back if you want to ask some more questions about it, but if you then want it exhibited, it must be produced to the Court, it will be marked for identification, and the Prosecution can then make any objections. Yes. Give it back to the accused. We'll give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, is there anything you want to add about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Even without seeing this book, this is not something that we have ever seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I know you haven't seen it, that's why you will have the chance to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: But we have absolutely no idea where it comes from or how it could be authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Of course. But let's have it in and we'll see what it's worth. We'll have a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Keep the book and then you'll be able to verify its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've turned the microphone off. We'll deal with this in an orderly fashion. Where is the book? Can we have the book. Mr. Milosevic, have you got the book back? Well, give it to the Court. Very well. We will now have a number for the book, marked for identification only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D162 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecution can have a look at it, and then they can make submissions. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true, in view of such a small number of people admitted into the hospital from the beginning until the 18th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He's answered that question. He can't give any further answers on the book. He knows nothing about it. He's never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't ask him about the book, Mr. May, but I am asking him whether it is true that numerous members of the National Guards Corps who were not wounded rushed to the hospital so that, organised by Dr. Vesna Bosanac and Dr. Navro, they put on bandages and plaster to present themselves as wounded so as to be transferred in that condition to territory under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That probably is not true. Now, whether there were individuals, it's quite possible, but this is just the product of imagination. But what is realistic is that the hospital was full of wounded during the conflict. It was packed full. It was overflowing. For anybody else to have to be added to give the impression that the hospital was full of the wounded, that is a distortion of the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your position on that matter is clear to me so I won't dwell on it any more. We have the evidence. On page 3, paragraph 7, you said that some soldiers who came to the hospital that day, judging by their uniforms and appearance, appeared to be members of the JNA whereas some were obviously not regular troops but were territorials. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Probably, yes, because that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you distinguish the regular JNA troops from volunteers and TO members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: In the first place, by the clothing they wore; their appearance and dress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm hurrying to make the best of my time. On page 5, paragraph 3, you said that during the night, you saw a soldier, Nikola Uglik, who was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with some men who were not regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That's what it looked like to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that because they had only parts of uniforms on them and strange caps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were in hospital, did you notice that any JNA soldier, that you could clearly set apart according to what you yourself said, that any JNA soldier was maltreating a patient, any hospital personnel or anyone there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice any mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also on page 4, paragraph 7, you say that the next morning at 7.30, buses arrived in front of the hospital guarded by young JNA soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that JNA members did not use any force, they were just standing next to the buses, in their regular capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: They used force in the sense of chasing people out, searching them and escorting them into the vehicles under threat of weapons, which is a kind of coercion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers were armed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Of course they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, but they were pointing their guns at the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you were transported by bus to the fairgrounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that that locality was under the control of the TO of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Actually, there was a barracks there, a barracks in Vukovar, and it was not in Croatian control. I'm referring to the Croatian military forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was under the control of members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: You can tell me that; I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that within that base you recognised a local citizen from Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that you stated then on page 5, paragraph 1, that in spite of threats you didn't see any force being used in relation to anyone in the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, except for verbal abuse. I didn't see any physical abuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that after waiting for two hours you were taken from there by bus to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, as you say, you had to pass through the so-called gauntlet of soldiers, you say, and members of paramilitary units who beat you. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Probably, yes, because that is what happened. Not just to me but all of us who were in those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on that occasion you managed, according to what you yourself say, to recognise a man who was a local tradesman from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. While waiting to get off, I saw this local man, businessman, from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you also saw many soldiers who had on their caps cockades or fur hats on their heads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those JNA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I don't belong to them, nor do I know, but they were probably organised together. They acted with the JNA and without the JNA. I didn't see their ID cards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I assume that you yourself must know that they couldn't have been members of the JNA wearing such insignia and fur hats, subaras [phoen].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, probably not. Maybe you can testify about that, who had what assignments and authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1171, in page 5, you say that inside the building you were in at Ovcara you noticed a man 50 to 60 years of age who was fat, and you assumed that he was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he looked like, because he was in full military dress, and he appeared to be -- I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that he was, on top, wearing something, a jacket.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: He was wearing a military wind jacket. The rest was military uniform, so from that one could conclude that he was an officer because he used his whistle to call people to order and he was issuing orders within the hangar in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you use the earlier criteria for distinguishing JNA members from others, could you say of him with certainty that he was a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: He appeared to be that. I can't say anything with certainty. I was not able to go up to anyone and ask him who he was and what he was, give me your IDs. This is just on the basis of my own observation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but people who were in the room with you, as you say on page 5 last paragraph, they were beaten by people who had parts of uniforms on them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't that clear that they were not JNA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: It is partly clear, but they were assisted by those who were wearing regular uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of everything that you have said, is it quite clear that Ovcara was not under the control of the JNA but by members of the TO or some paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No. I can't come to that conclusion because it was co-organised. They were assisting one another or acting together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All those that you have described, you described as people who could not be JNA members. Never mind. But you say there were about 300 prisoner at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Up to or about. As for the commander. He was some sort of a military JNA organised person. At least that's what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you knew many of the prisoners but not well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Some of them well, some of them not so well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many of them were your co-fighters and members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: None of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. So you were the only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, the only one. No, the only one from my unit. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that in a group of 15 to 20 from Ovcara you were transferred by truck somewhere else, and in addition to you there was a driver and a soldier with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No soldiers or so-called soldier was next to me but only those who were being transported, and we were being moved with the explanation that you were -- that we were going to another hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a two-tonne truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: In any event, it was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a civilian truck or a military truck judging by licence plates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Quite certainly a JNA truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person who was with you as escort, the only soldier, did he look to you like a JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: He was not an escort. He was there only to we were boarding the truck. Later on, he sat next to the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he look like a JNA member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: An olive-grey uniform. I can't be more precise. But he was a soldier because he was in a uniform and wearing a regular soldier's cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that Ovcara in those days was under the control of members of the TO and certain paramilitary units and not the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I can't know that, but we were commanded after all by members of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see commanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That man with the whistle. And he had a command role, in my assessment and judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Major Sljivancanin anywhere at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know him. Only later on from the media I saw who he was. I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No, I didn't. At least I didn't know him, and I didn't notice him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you managed to escape from the truck, in the village of Trznice the next day you were again arrested by a group of five of what you call Chetniks. Page 7, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said Trznice? The village of Trznice does not exist. What paragraph are you referring to, what page? You have erroneous information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On -- it is on page 7, paragraph 5. I can't find it right away, but I can't lose any more time. I'm just noting that's where it is. Is it true that they didn't beat you either own though you admitted after some time that you were a fugitive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: They didn't, but they took me to their headquarters where I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then those men later on handed you over to regular military policemen, as you call them. I assume they were regular JNA members.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, some kind of military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that from there JNA members transferred you to Sid and from there to the military prison if Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. First they beat me up well in the basement and then they interrogated me. I testified being handcuffed to the radiator and then the next day with several other prisoners, members of the National Guards Corps probably, I was transferred to Sid. After Sid, to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that no one touched you at the military prison in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that before you reached the military prison they beat you and brutally I think is what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. But this happened on a number of occasions. I was all black and blue from the beating. And the military policemen beat me most at Stari Jankovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you lease look - I won't put it on the ELMO because the witness is protected, but look here, I have a list of photographed convicted persons at the military court in Belgrade and there under certain number, I won't even mention the number, but page will be open for you to see it, under the next number is -- first you, then another person you mention with you. Then again further on there is here quite a number of persons from a list. I have 31 here on the list. Photographs of persons convicted at the military Tribunal in Belgrade. So please check whether this is you and your colleague. You can look at the photographs of the others too, if you wish, and please tell me, do you recognise anyone from those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: [redacted]. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone else from that list and from those photographs of those convicted by the military Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when were those photographs taken, as soon as you arrived at the military Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Not straight away but very shortly after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look closely at the photographs and tell me whether on any one of you any injuries are visible, since you said that they beat you on the head, et cetera. Are there any visible injuries on any one of you, because the photographs were taken in the Tribunal after these things happened to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: If you wanted to see what we looked like, you should obtain photographs -- you should have shown photographs taken in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, 1171, but these photographs were taken immediately after you arrive at the military Tribunal in Belgrade. So look at all the photographs of all those persons, and there are 31 of them. Are there any visible injuries on any one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Do you know when I arrived at the military investigating prison? Do you know when I reached it? How much time had gone by from the moment I was captured, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No, several months. I was detained far before I ever reached the military investigating prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we can compare those dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, we can indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clear up one more point. I asked you when we were speaking about the Serb facilities in Vukovar which were destroyed with the anti-armoured devices that we mentioned, I asked you whether anybody had shot at those facilities prior to that, and your answer was no. Now, is there any doubt that the facilities that were destroyed and whose proprietors were Serbs, that they couldn't have represented a military target of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to comment, nor do I know what facilities you're referring to or what period of time. It's not up to me to bring a judgement about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't read from the list the catering establishments, the names of the catering establishments because I didn't want to jeopardise your identity, but you had the documents in your hands, and you were able to see that the month we were discussing was October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over this -- we've on over it, and it doesn't seem any point going back to it now. We've her the witness's answers and he can't say any more than he has done. If you've got some evidence about it, Mr. Milosevic, you can call it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer one more question for me, please, Mr. 1171. Do you have any information as to how many Serbs you personally killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I never killed a single Serb, so that is absolutely absurd, and the question is improper too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said civilians were killed from -- as a result of the devices that you positioned in Vukovar yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: They were soldiers who attacked the town. Those were the ones who were killed. And that has nothing to do with my actions as a private person but as part of the military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the devices you planted in the civilian parts of town predominantly inhabited by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has already dealt with this, and your time is now up. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you got any questions? Just five minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll hurry up. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you have the statement of the 14th of June in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me have a look. Give me a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at page 3, the last paragraph there or, rather, the penultimate paragraph begins with the word "Major." And I'm just going to deal with your entrance into the hospital and the incident with the truck. You don't have to explain anything else to Their Honours. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, "Major."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Before you entered the hospital, you said you noticed a Major and the insignia he had. He seemed to you to be an officer, "And I remember his face and I'm quite certain that I would recognise him from a photograph or if I saw any records of him." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "It appeared that that man was in command of everything and issued orders." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that man wasn't Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. Quite definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at the other page. "During at that stage I did not see a single person using force of any kind." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And then the last sentence after that it says: "The soldiers weren't there for a long time. When I decided to go into the hospital." That means at the point you entered the hospital there were no soldiers there any more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: That's not true. The soldiers had taken over the hospital space and from that point in time they were in the hospital all the time. And they provided security outside the hospital, and nobody was allowed entrance. They controlled everything that went on there and the comings and goings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself went into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: I was in the hospital all the time. We're speaking about the hospital compound, but I spoke about the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to get through what I have. You said, "I went to the basement and joined my men there who were wounded and in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes. That's the hospital building in the basement of the hospital building. But what I'm talking about happened in the hospital compound, outside the actual hospital building. Perhaps that's where the misunderstanding lies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you describe how you fled from the truck, and you gave a statement to the organs of the Croatian -- or, rather the Croatian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorities. I have the statement. It was served on me by the Prosecution. Could you now have a look at it and especially the portion where you say the following: "I sat at the back of the truck. There were no guards in the truck, so before we arrived at our destination, I was able to jump off the truck." Could you have a look at that passage, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement and what do you find to challenge there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, you didn't mention a guard. The guard was the co-driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't at the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't say there were any guards in the truck there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Not in the back part where the detainees were, but of course there was a guard. He opened the truck for us and then went to sit next to the driver. So he was there to provide security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said that when the investigators asked you, but you didn't mention that in that statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: All right. Maybe I didn't describe it that way or perhaps I wasn't legally clear enough in legal terms, but I'm repeating it now and you'll be able to get an image and picture of what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain this to me: You said that the truck veered off left into a field and that it ran at 10 to 20 kilometres an hour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, how fast truck was going I can't say. That's my assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say somebody warned you and said, "They'll kill us all. And then it was only you who jumped out when the truck was moving at a speed of 10 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No, that wasn't me. Somebody wanted to jump off the truck but the others stopped him and prevented him from jumping off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Re-Examined by Mr. McKeon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that the person who -- the JNA soldier who was helping load you onto the truck was wearing a regular soldier's cap. Could you describe the cap that he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, it was an army cap of the former JNA. The kind the former JNA wore. It was olive-green in colour with the five-pointed star up in the front. I don't know how to describe it in other terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about injuries that may be shown on this photograph. Did you suffer any bruises or injuries from the beatings that you described you received at Sremska Mitrovica; and if so, on what part of your body were those bruises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: The bruises were all over my body, but I was all black and blue on my head because I was kicked with a boot when I was being transferred from Sid to Mitrovica. Not just me but everybody else. We were all kicked directly in our -- in the head, and that's when they knocked my teeth out. And I was black and blue all over, so I looked like a raccoon. I was all black and blue. And my body was already black and blue because they -- I received the bruises in Stari Jankovci when two soldiers, members of the military police with white belts beat me up so badly that I was all black and blue, covered in bruises and found it difficult to move at all. And they took a photograph of me in Sremska Mitrovica, and there is photographic evidence there, if it hasn't gone off somewhere else. But there's a picture of me looking like I did at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was it between the time that that photograph was taken and you received this beating and this photograph you were shown was taken in the Belgrade prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Well, at least two to three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you received bruises in Stari Jankovci from two soldiers, members of the military police with white belts. Was it one of those military policemen who asked you about what you knew about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked me much of anything over there and not that detailed. They just beat us to beat us up. The reason wasn't important, who or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Sremska Mitrovica, were you asked to sign or write out a written statement describing your activities laying mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Yes, they did ask that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of that, did you draw a diagram for them showing them where mines were laid to assist in demining the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1171
utterances.text: Correct. Everything I was able to recollect to help them in a way, to help them locate the position of the mines which I and my soldiers laid, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions other than making a brief submission on this Exhibit D161. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, make your submission about this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would object to this coming into evidence because, first of all, there's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, let me interrupt you. We have only marked it for identification. We have not admitted it, for the reasons which you have raised. Now, let's have the document. You can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I have looked at it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. If you want to make further investigation, you can. If you don't, it remains marked for identification, but it remains in that way until it's proved and admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Witness C-1171, thank you for coming back to the Tribunal to give your evidence again. It's now concluded, and you are free to go. Would you just wait a moment while the blinds are put down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I ask a question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it, and I'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an indictment from a court in Belgrade charging me, and I'd like to show it to you, and I have what was published in the press in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I suggest is you speak to Mr. McKeon about it afterwards, and if it -- he thinks it should go in, then he can apply to put it in on Monday. He can draw it to our attention. We'll deal with it in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
